tagline: The person who keeps tech projects moving — schedules, scope, stakeholders, and the notes everyone actually reads.
what_you_do: You keep IT projects on track without writing the code yourself. Day to day you coordinate schedules and dependencies, gather and document what the business actually needs, translate between technical teams and everyone else, chase down blockers, and run the meetings — standups, planning, retros — that keep work visible. It's one of the few genuine non-coder first roles in tech: employers hire coordinators and junior business analysts for organization and communication, then teach them the domain.
day_in_life: Run the morning standup and capture blockers before they become slipped deadlines
Sit with a business stakeholder to pin down what 'the report should be faster' actually means, then write it up as requirements
Update the project plan after a vendor delay and walk the team through what moves
Translate a developer's technical constraint into plain language for the steering committee
Chase three people for the sign-offs the project can't proceed without

salary.entry: ~$59,830 to start — coordinator and junior BA roles sit at the bottom of the range
salary.growth: +6% for project specialists; the analyst track (median $103,790) is growing faster at +9%
salary.note: U.S. BLS figures for Project Management Specialists (13-1082) and Computer Systems Analysts (15-1211); a median is the midpoint of everyone employed, so entry pay runs well below it. Verify against the live BLS pages before deciding.

downsides: You carry responsibility for the deadline without authority over the people who can miss it. Herding stakeholders, absorbing scope creep, and translating for both sides all day is genuinely tiring — and when a project slips, the coordinator is the visible face of it. Early roles can be heavy on note-taking and chasing before you earn real ownership.

fits_if: You're naturally organized and people trust you to follow through
You like talking to people all day and turning conversations into structure
You want into tech without making coding your job
less_ideal_if: You want deep, heads-down technical work with minimal meetings
Chasing people for updates would drain you
You need clear authority to feel effective — this role runs on influence

skills.name: Written and verbal communication
skills.note: The core tool of the job — clear notes, clear asks, clear status.

skills.name: Organization & scheduling
skills.note: Dependencies, milestones, and who's waiting on whom.

skills.name: Requirements elicitation & documentation
skills.note: Asking the questions that turn a vague wish into something a team can build.

skills.name: Agile & waterfall fundamentals
skills.note: Enough to run ceremonies and know which method fits which project.

skills.name: Data literacy (SQL basics, reading dashboards)
skills.note: What separates coordinators from analysts — and raises your ceiling.

certs.title: Google Project Management Certificate
certs.reason: Builds the vocabulary and a portfolio capstone — banks 100+ PMI education hours and takes $175 off the CAPM exam that follows.

certs.title: PMI CAPM
certs.reason: PMI's genuine foundation cert — the recognized entry signal for project roles (PMP comes later, after documented experience).

certs.title: Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I)
certs.reason: The no-course-required Scrum credential with lifetime validity — ideal if the jobs you're seeing are agile teams.

certs.title: ITIL 4 Foundation
certs.reason: The IT service-management vocabulary enterprises run on — strongest for service desk and ITSM-adjacent coordination.

cert_note: Honest priority check: this is a portfolio-first path — evidence you've coordinated real work beats any credential. Pick ONE of these to match the jobs you're actually seeing locally; PMP is not entry-level (it requires documented project experience first).

trial.objective: Do the actual job on a real-life project — a move, an event, a trip: elicit what people need, structure a plan with milestones and risks in a spreadsheet, and get someone to agree to it.
trial.disclosure: Fully local — any spreadsheet you already have; nothing installed or transmitted.

roadmap.title: Learn the vocabulary
roadmap.focus: Agile, Scrum, and waterfall basics plus the tooling — free via Scrum.org's Scrum Guide, Atlassian's agile guides, and a Jira free tier. Learn to build a real project plan in a spreadsheet.

roadmap.title: Build coordination evidence
roadmap.focus: Coordinate something real: a volunteer project, a community event, a process fix at your current job. Document the requirements, the plan, the risks, and the outcome — that write-up is your portfolio.

roadmap.title: Add an entry credential
roadmap.focus: CAPM, PSM I, or ITIL 4 Foundation — pick the one matching the jobs you're seeing locally. These validate the vocabulary; your portfolio proves you can use it.

roadmap.title: Pick your lane
roadmap.focus: Project management (toward PMP once you have the experience it requires), business analysis (add SQL and data skills), or platform ownership (become the Jira/M365 person). Each is a real career, not just a rung.

adjacent_paths.reason: BA work and analytics share the requirements-and-evidence mindset.
Coordinators who learn the collaboration platform often grow into administering it.
